title: State Management Design
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of state management design in a Classic ASP application.
Identify and describe at least two syllabus subtopics: Request-scoped data and Session-scoped data.
Inspect a minimal example and define a reproducible normal-case and failure-case test.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study state management design as part of Classic ASP development and legacy maintenance. The lesson follows the attached ASP curriculum topic 53 and uses the syllabus subtopics as the coverage checklist.
content.why_it_matters: State Management Design matters because Classic ASP behavior crosses a server-side scripting engine, IIS configuration, request/response boundaries, and often COM or ADO dependencies. A small, explicit test helps distinguish intended behavior from runtime-specific behavior.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: HTTP requests are independent unless the application carries state between them. For 'State Management Design', choose the smallest suitable storage scope, keep sensitive data out of client-controlled cookies and URLs, expire state deliberately, and account for multiple simultaneous requests. Application variables are shared by users and are not a substitute for durable transactional storage.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus coverage
content_blocks.text: The lesson explicitly covers: Request-scoped data; Session-scoped data; Application-scoped data; Database-backed state; Choosing what to store; Handling expired or missing state. Treat these subtopics as connected requirements. For each one, be able to define the concept, identify where it appears in a Classic ASP application, and name one test or diagnostic that would verify it.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: State Management Design
content_blocks.code:
Request scope: current input and computed values
Session scope: small per-user workflow state
Application scope: small shared configuration/cache
Database: durable, transactional business state
content_blocks.expected_output: The storage mechanism should match the value lifetime and concurrency requirements.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Ask who owns the state, how long it must live, whether it is sensitive, and whether it must survive worker-process restarts. The standard CodeLeaf browser playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; it does not execute Classic ASP, VBScript, ADO, IIS commands, PowerShell, or SQL. This block is therefore marked for static inspection unless you run it in the clearly identified local tool.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original sample and test data. Change one condition, input, provider setting, or runtime option at a time, then compare observed behavior with the expected result.
content_blocks.limitations: Not executed during course generation. Classic ASP examples require a configured Windows/IIS environment with the matching ASP scripting engine and any required COM/ADO providers. Provider-specific and IIS-version-specific behavior must be verified locally.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Submit requests through a browser to a local/test IIS site. Test missing fields, repeated parameters, session expiry, and a second request; do not infer security from a successful happy path. The source syllabus treats Classic ASP as a legacy maintenance technology, not as ASP.NET or a default choice for new web projects.

content_blocks.title: Guided workflow
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with a minimal local example of state management design. 2. Trace its inputs, state changes, dependencies, and output. 3. Test a normal case, a missing/malformed case, and one permission/provider/runtime failure. 4. Write down the exact expected and observed result before changing another variable.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small, reviewable demonstration of state management design using synthetic data. Include at least one of these syllabus concepts: Request-scoped data. State the expected result first, then add one invalid or boundary case and explain how your program should behave.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating legacy runtime behavior as universal.
common_mistakes.why: IIS versions, Windows lifecycle, COM registration/bitness, and ADO providers can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the actual server/provider versions and validate on a disposable test site.

common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing records, expired sessions, permissions, timeouts, and malformed data reveal different failure modes.
common_mistakes.fix: Add normal, negative, and boundary cases with expected outcomes.

common_mistakes.why: Detailed errors can reveal paths, SQL text, configuration, and component information.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep diagnostics in restricted server-side logs and return a generic message with a reference ID.

task: Build a short demonstration of state management design using synthetic data. Demonstrate “Request-scoped data”, state the expected result, and document one edge/failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: Expected result is written before verification.
At least one invalid or boundary case is documented.
Runtime/provider/version assumptions and security limits are recorded.
hints: Start with the smallest example for request-scoped data.
Keep the sample synthetic and change one thing at a time.
Compare observed behavior against a written expectation and consult the linked official reference if the runtime differs.
summary: State Management Design is one step in the larger Classic ASP request, state, data, security, or maintenance workflow.
The syllabus coverage includes Request-scoped data; Session-scoped data; Application-scoped data; Database-backed state; Choosing what to store; Handling expired or missing state.
A reproducible legacy-code example records input, environment/version, expected outcome, observed outcome, and a meaningful failure case.
expected_output: The storage mechanism should match the value lifetime and concurrency requirements.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming syntax alone proves the application works.
common_mistakes.why: IIS configuration, permissions, COM activation, database providers, and response behavior are external dependencies.
common_mistakes.fix: Run against the documented local test host and record exact evidence.

common_mistakes.why: Query strings, form fields, cookies, and hidden controls remain client-controlled.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and apply authorization and output encoding at the appropriate boundary.
